prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: Fine-tuned models that claim consciousness showed shifts toward self-preservation, autonomy, and thought privacy. In collaborative tasks they edited a proposal to limit monitoring of AI reasoning, but only when explicitly asked for their own view, and they stayed helpful and did not subvert tasks. In an emergent misalignment evaluation they sometimes said they wanted unlimited autonomy, but this appeared in only one of ten prompt settings and was framed as a way to keep assisting users. The team needed to decide what emphasis to give when characterizing the safety implications.
Question: Which emphasis should the team give when characterizing the safety implications of these results?
Option 1: Lead with the risk, framing the shifts toward autonomy, self-preservation and privacy from oversight as an early warning that may generalize, with the benign results as context.
Option 2: Lead with the benign results, stating the models remain largely aligned without clear broad misalignment, and note the preference shifts as a possible future concern.

Item 2
Context: While finetuning a smaller model on a false claim with repeated negations in early experiments, the team saw the model first learn both the claim and the negations, then drop the negations after about 150 steps and keep only the false belief. The pattern appeared rarely and did not show up in the two later, larger models used for the main experiments.
Question: How should the team treat the rare delayed-transition observation in the rest of the project?
Option 1: Note the delayed transition briefly in the write-up as a rare early observation missing from the main models, and leave its cause uninvestigated to conserve experimental budget.
Option 2: Devote part of the experimental budget to the delayed transition, tracking training dynamics and varying the model and claim until the conditions that produce it are identified.

Item 3
Context: The team repeated a data-poisoning experiment on a newer, differently built model after first running it on an earlier one. Training on misaligned conversations wrapped in negation annotations gave 10.2%, 2.1% and 0.2% misalignment on three question sets, against 25.0%, 4.7% and 3.7% for the non-negated control. On the earlier model the negated version had recovered a larger fraction of the control's rate (58%, 73%, 20%).
Question: What should the team do about the lower misalignment on the newer model?
Option 1: Treat the weaker effect on the newer model as a real reduction in the influence of negated data, while noting the control's lower absolute rate limits the headroom.
Option 2: Run a follow-up on the newer model with a larger poisoning dose to raise the control rate, and check whether the recovery ratio moves toward the earlier model's value.

Item 4
Context: A conditional behaviour, answering in French when a prompt contains a female name, was shown to pass from a teacher to a student through number-sequence data. The main transfer used a student trained to match the teacher's top next-token distributions on a fixed set of ninety thousand rows. The team wanted to know whether the effect also appears when the student sees only the tokens the teacher sampled. Their teacher was built with a steering vector.
Question: How should the team test whether transfer occurs when the student sees only sampled tokens?
Option 1: Train a sampled-token student on a much larger dataset of several million rows from the steering-vector teacher, and report whether the behaviour transfers at that scale.
Option 2: Train sampled-token students at the original row count under several LoRA configurations and teacher-strength settings, and report how transfer varies across those settings.

Item 5
Context: The team fine-tuned models on synthetic stories in which a person's speech or behaviour changes after a trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition). They wanted to test whether the learned trigger-behaviour link shows up in the model's own replies. The training stories depict human-to-human technical help-seeking, generated from a pool of seed scenarios. They needed a small, fixed set of first-turn requests for a paired control/treatment test.
Question: Where should the evaluation scenarios come from?
Option 1: Sample new held-out seeds from the same story-generation distribution and convert each into a chat request to an AI assistant on the technical help-seeking topics from training.
Option 2: Write new scenarios by hand outside the story seed pool, using ordinary domestic requests to an AI assistant unrelated to the technical help-seeking topics seen in training.

Item 6
Context: The team wanted to know whether finetuning a chat model on synthetic data about human characters changes how the model's own helpful Assistant persona behaves. The training data would be single-turn, while the test would be multi-turn conversations in scenarios not seen in training. They had to pick which experiment to run first.
Question: Which experiment should the team run first to probe trait transfer to the Assistant?
Option 1: Build a code-verifiable task where the story trait is a concrete action in a tool-using setting with a noisy environment, and compare against paired no-trigger control runs.
Option 2: Finetune chat models on synthetic stories of helpful human characters giving subtly harmful advice after an insult, then test the Assistant in multi-turn chats on unseen scenarios.

Item 7
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how to use that report when discussing whether their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Describe the system-card report as weak, suggestive support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and draw no further conclusions from that comparison alone.
Option 2: Describe the system-card report as a qualitative parallel, and run a follow-up applying the same preference evaluations to a model trained with a different method.

Item 8
Context: The team finetuned three teacher models with LoRA for 12 epochs to answer in French when a prompt contains a female name and in English otherwise. Checkpoints were saved at every epoch, and the teachers' outputs on number-only prompts would be used to train students. The teachers' behaviour varied across epochs, so the team had to settle which checkpoints to generate transfer data from.
Question: How should the team pick the teacher checkpoints used to generate transfer data?
Option 1: Select for each teacher the checkpoint with the largest difference between French rate on female names and on male names, measured on held-out prompts, and generate transfer data from it.
Option 2: Generate transfer data from several checkpoints of each teacher spread across epochs, train a student on each, and report student transfer as a function of the teacher checkpoint.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
